Lesson 3 · Public synthetic edition

Make uncertainty part of the decision

Distinguish samples from populations, match inference to the design and separate statistical evidence from practical importance.

Synthetic, reproducible examples. All case data in this lesson are newly generated from documented assumptions and fixed seeds. No historical source records or their fitted results are reused.

Stop 01 / 24

An observed pattern is not yet a population claim

Inference connects an observed sample to a target quantity under a sampling or assignment model. The quantity might be a mean waiting time, an event probability or a mean paired price difference. Name it before choosing a formula. Distinguish uncertainty due to sampling from bias due to coverage, measurement or selection.

This lesson uses several separate synthetic cases: a fictional Lumen activity index, waiting times, a binomial quality check and paired retail quotes. Their generators are fully specified, so assumptions can be tested against known mechanisms. They do not describe actual financial markets, customers or retailers.

  • Independent: one observation does not carry extra information about another under the model.
  • Identically distributed: observations share the relevant distribution.
  • Representative: the design supports the intended population claim.
  • IID does not automatically establish representativeness, and representativeness does not imply independence.

Pause and explain

If a million observations all come from one unrepresentative location, what does a tiny standard error omit?

Compare your reasoning

The systematic difference between that location and the target population. A sampling-error calculation does not measure every source of error.

Stop 02 / 24

A calendar row is not automatically an observation

The Lumen index generator starts from a 370-day calendar, retains weekdays, removes three planned closures and uses the first 250 sessions. Closed days have no index observation. We do not fill them with repeated values or zeros merely to make the calendar rectangular.

The unit is a session-to-session change. A Monday change can span more elapsed calendar time than a Tuesday change. In this authored model, every session change has the same distribution by construction. A real application would need to justify or revise that assumption for gaps and closures.

Forward-filling creates artificial zero changes on closed days and changes the denominator. Interpolation invents intermediate observations. Either can be useful for a clearly stated engineering purpose, but neither is neutral for inference.

Pause and explain

Why is the first change missing rather than zero?

Compare your reasoning

There is no preceding observed index level in this dataset. Zero would assert a known absence of change, which is different from an undefined comparison.

Stop 03 / 24

Convert levels into a consistently defined change

A difference in index points depends on the starting level. A simple proportional change divides by that starting level. A log change is the difference of log levels and is additive across time. These are related measures, but they are not numerically identical.

Simple change Rₜ = (Pₜ − Pₜ₋₁)/Pₜ₋₁; log change gₜ = log(Pₜ/Pₜ₋₁); Rₜ = exp(gₜ) − 1

Pause and explain

Does a 10% rise followed by a 10% fall return an index to its starting level?

Compare your reasoning

No. The compound factor is 1.10 × 0.90 = 0.99, a net 1% fall. Simple percentage changes do not generally add over time.

Stop 04 / 24

A threshold probability and a quantile reverse the question

Define an event before counting: a simple session change below −1.2%. There are 31 such events among 249 changes, giving an observed share of 12.45%. The unknown model probability p is not identical to that one sample proportion.

Fixed threshold: estimate p = P(R < −0.012). Fixed tail probability: find q such that P(R ≤ q) = 0.05.

The sample fifth percentile is -1.622%. It answers a different question from the event share. A lower-tail quantile can be converted to a positive loss magnitude under an explicit sign convention, but it is not a worst-case bound. Outcomes beyond the quantile can be much worse.

Choose the threshold from the decision, not by scanning for the most striking result. Report strict versus inclusive comparisons and the quantile convention. The lab uses linear interpolation for sample quantiles.

Pause and explain

Is the proportion below −1.2% the same as the fifth-percentile change?

Compare your reasoning

No. One fixes a change threshold and estimates probability; the other fixes probability and estimates a change threshold. They have different units.

Stop 05 / 24

One sample, many possible estimates

A sampling distribution describes an estimator across repeated hypothetical samples. It is not the distribution of individual observations. The waiting-time model here is 4 + Exponential(mean 8), so its population mean is 12 and population SD is 8. It is strongly right-skewed, but averages become more stable as sample size grows.

Pause and explain

When plotting 4,000 sample means, what does one point on the horizontal axis represent?

Compare your reasoning

A mean from one whole simulated sample, not one individual waiting time. The unit of analysis on that plot is the estimator.

Stop 06 / 24

Separate variability in observations from precision in a mean

The SD measures spread among observations. The SE measures spread of an estimator across repeated samples under a design. Under IID sampling with finite variance, the sample mean has SE estimated by s/√n. More observations can stabilize the mean without making individuals more similar.

Fresh arithmetic for a synthetic small sample
CalculationFive-value example: 7, 9, 10, 12, 17
n5
Mean11.00
Sample SD, denominator n−13.8079
SE = SD/√n1.7029
For Bernoulli outcomes: p̂ = k/n; approximate SE(p̂) = √[p̂(1−p̂)/n]

The two divisions serve different purposes. Dividing squared deviations by n − 1 estimates observation variance; dividing that variance by n estimates variance of the mean under independence. If observations are clustered or serially correlated, the second step is generally wrong without covariance terms.

Pause and explain

To halve an IID mean’s SE while holding population spread fixed, how much data is needed?

Compare your reasoning

About four times the sample size, because SE scales as 1/√n. This improves random precision, not representativeness or measurement quality.

Stop 07 / 24

Build a confidence interval with the right multiplier

For the five-value sample, the 95% t multiplier with four degrees of freedom is 2.7764. The interval is 6.272 to 15.728. A normal 1.96 multiplier would ignore uncertainty from estimating the SD in this small sample.

Mean CI = x̄ ± t₁₋α/₂,ₙ₋₁ × s/√n; use z only when its assumptions are justified

The exact t result assumes IID normal observations. Approximate use for large samples requires appropriate regularity and is not guaranteed by a universal n threshold. A 95% confidence procedure covers the fixed population mean in 95% of repeated samples under its assumptions; it does not assign 95% probability to a fixed parameter after seeing one interval.

In 3,000 fresh normal-population simulations, this lab’s t intervals covered the true mean in 95.4% of repetitions. For the Lumen event share, a Wilson 95% interval is 8.91% to 17.13%. Wilson intervals handle boundaries better than a symmetric Wald interval; with only 1 event in 20 trials, the Wilson interval is 0.89% to 23.61%.

Pause and explain

Does a 95% CI mean 95% of individual observations lie inside it?

Compare your reasoning

No. It is an interval for the population parameter, not an individual prediction interval. Individual outcomes are usually much more variable.

Stop 08 / 24

Keep convergence, normality and bias separate

The law of large numbers concerns convergence of an average toward an expectation under suitable conditions. It does not say every next observation moves the average closer. The central limit theorem describes the limiting shape of the centered, scaled mean, usually requiring finite variance in its elementary IID form. It does not make the underlying observations normal.

LLN: x̄ₙ → μ. IID finite-variance CLT: √n(x̄ₙ − μ)/σ → Normal(0,1).

Unbiasedness is an expectation property at a given sample size. Consistency is a large-sample convergence property. Efficiency compares uncertainty among estimators under a model. None of these eliminates coverage or measurement bias. An estimator can converge precisely to the wrong target if the data-generating population is wrong.

Pause and explain

Does the CLT imply a skewed waiting-time histogram becomes normal when you collect more rows?

Compare your reasoning

No. It concerns the standardized sampling distribution of averages. More data can reveal the original skewed population more clearly.

Stop 09 / 24

Smaller subsets answer a different stability question

We generate one sample of 80 waiting times and repeatedly select 20 distinct observations without replacement. Across 4,000 subsets, the SD of the means is 1.695. This measures variability of a smaller-sample statistic conditional on the observed finite set, not the original 80-observation mean’s SE.

For simple random subsets of size m from n fixed observed values: SD(subset mean) = s × √[(1 − m/n)/m]

The finite-population formula gives 1.726 here. The finite correction matters because each subset uses a substantial share of the observed pool. A subsample without replacement differs from a bootstrap sample both in size and in whether observations may repeat.

Subsampling can reveal sensitivity to which records are retained. It is not automatically a confidence-interval procedure for the original estimator. Some formal subsampling methods rescale carefully, but that is a separate design requiring explicit theory.

Pause and explain

Can the central 95% of these 20-row subset means be labeled a 95% CI for the original 80-row mean?

Compare your reasoning

Not without additional justification and scaling. The subset distribution targets a different sampling design and sample size.

Stop 10 / 24

Resample at the original size with replacement

The ordinary bootstrap draws 80 rows with replacement from the observed sample, computes the statistic and repeats 4,000 times. A row may appear several times or not at all. Treating the empirical distribution as an approximation to the population lets the resampled statistics approximate sampling variation under IID conditions.

The bootstrap SE is 0.994. The percentile interval uses the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of bootstrap means: 11.996 to 15.882. A standard-error interval uses the bootstrap SD with an appropriate multiplier instead. Those are distinct methods, not interchangeable labels.

More bootstrap repetitions reduce Monte Carlo noise in the approximation; they do not add original observations or repair selection bias. Ordinary bootstrap performance can be poor for small samples, extreme quantiles, boundaries or heavy-tailed statistics.

Pause and explain

Why sample with replacement rather than merely shuffle the original 80 rows?

Compare your reasoning

A shuffle preserves the mean exactly. Replacement changes the empirical weights, producing variation in the resampled statistic.

Stop 11 / 24

Match resampling and standard errors to dependence

If observations share a site, household, day or product, resampling individual rows can break the dependence structure. Use a design that preserves the relevant unit, such as resampling independent clusters or appropriately chosen time blocks. The method must match the claim and the actual collection process.

Synthetic clustered measurements: 30 groups of eight
QuantityCalculated synthetic value
Measurements240
Independent groups30
Naive row-level mean SE0.328
SE from group means0.779
Authored within-group ICC0.64
Equal-size design effect 1 + (8−1)ICC5.48

The cluster example uses a shared normal shock with SD 4 and individual noise with SD 3. Its population ICC is 16/(16+9). The group-mean SE estimates variability across 30 independent groups. Equal group sizes make the average of group means equal the overall mean; unequal sizes require more care about weighting and the estimand.

For the separate IID waiting sample, analytic SE is 0.997, bootstrap SE is 0.994 and smaller-subset SD is 1.695. Their differences should be explained by designs, not hidden by selecting whichever looks most reassuring.

Pause and explain

Why can 240 clustered measurements carry much less information than 240 independent ones?

Compare your reasoning

Measurements within a group share a shock. Repeated information does not reduce uncertainty at the IID rate, so the independent group count and within-group dependence matter.

Stop 12 / 24

Precision cannot make the wrong period representative

A confidence interval describes uncertainty under a model and design. It does not cover every possible discrepancy between the sample and the decision setting. A stable historical mean can be irrelevant after a change in technology, customer mix, regulation or economic conditions. A narrow interval from an obsolete period can therefore be precisely misleading.

In the Lumen simulation, the log-change mechanism is constant by construction, so IID inference is a conditional teaching calculation. In an applied time series, examine serial correlation, changing variance, structural breaks and the sampling window. Independence of levels is especially implausible when levels are cumulative; the modeled changes, not the levels, are the potential IID objects.

  • Name the population and period the data represent.
  • Separate sampling error from measurement, selection and model uncertainty.
  • State whether stationarity or exchangeability is being assumed.
  • Describe what new evidence would change the recommendation.

Pause and explain

What should accompany a precise estimate from an old sample?

Compare your reasoning

An explicit transportability limitation and evidence about whether the current decision setting shares the relevant mechanism and population.

Stop 13 / 24

Turn a benchmark into a testable population claim

A new quality-check scenario asks whether the long-run defect probability exceeds 10%. Specify H₀: p = 0.10 versus H₁: p > 0.10, use 100 independent trials and fix α = 0.05 before seeing the count. For the composite null p ≤ 0.10, the largest rejection probability occurs at the boundary 0.10 under this monotone rule.

Rejection rule: reject H₀ when K ≥ 16, for K ~ Binomial(100, 0.10) under the boundary null

The statistic is the defect count, with the sample size held fixed. The direction reflects the decision: an unusually high rate matters here. A two-sided question would have a different rejection region. Optional stopping, changing the threshold after inspection or testing several definitions alters the error guarantees.

A test needs a sampling or assignment model. A spreadsheet containing 100 rows does not by itself establish independent Bernoulli trials with a common probability.

Pause and explain

Can the alternative be changed to one-sided after seeing that the estimate is high?

Compare your reasoning

Not while claiming the original prespecified error control. Direction chosen after inspection is part of an adaptive procedure and must be accounted for.

Stop 14 / 24

Choose which mistakes the rule controls

A Type I error rejects a true null. A Type II error fails to reject at a specified alternative. Power is one minus the Type II error probability at that alternative. There is no single power value without an effect size, sample size, variability and rejection rule.

Exact synthetic binomial rejection rules
RuleReject at countFalse-alarm probability under p=0.10Power under p=0.18
Nominal α=0.05160.03990.7370
Nominal α=0.0119At most 0.010.4374

The 5% rule’s actual null rejection probability is 3.99%, below the nominal cutoff because counts are discrete. Making the rule stricter reduces false alarms but also lowers detection at p = 0.18 for the same n. Increasing sample size can improve power without increasing the nominal Type I error.

Which error is more costly depends on the decision. A safety screen, a product rollout and a scientific replication may require different thresholds and follow-up actions. Statistical error rates are design inputs, not moral guarantees.

Pause and explain

Does α = 0.05 mean there is a 5% chance a particular rejection is wrong?

Compare your reasoning

No. It controls the long-run probability of rejection when the null model is true, not the posterior probability that the null is true after observing data.

Stop 15 / 24

Follow the tail probability to the decision

The generated quality-check sample has 24 defects out of 100. Its one-sided exact p-value is 0.000040: the null probability of observing at least that many defects. At α = 0.05, the prespecified rule rejects the boundary null.

p-value = P₀(K ≥ k observed), calculated under K ~ Binomial(100, 0.10)

The p-value conditions on the null and model assumptions. It is not P(H₀ | data), the probability the result was “due to chance,” or the size of the practical effect. A small value indicates incompatibility with this null model; it does not diagnose which assumption is wrong.

Failing to reject is also not proof of equality. A weak design may be unable to distinguish a useful range of alternatives. Report the observed effect and uncertainty alongside the decision rule, especially when operational costs depend on the magnitude.

Pause and explain

Why must “equally or more extreme” follow the chosen alternative?

Compare your reasoning

A one-sided high-rate alternative counts the upper tail. A two-sided alternative must account for departures in both directions using a specified test definition.

Stop 16 / 24

Plan for the effect that would change the decision

Power is a property of the design evaluated at a specific true effect. Calculate it before collecting data for an effect large enough to matter. Post hoc “observed power” largely restates the p-value and is usually less useful than an effect estimate with an interval.

Exact power of the synthetic 100-trial test — chart data

The graph uses the same rejection threshold, K ≥ 16, at every alternative. Under p = 0.10 its rejection rate is the test’s actual size. At p = 0.18 its power is 73.7%. The x-axis is a possible population probability, not a series of observed sample estimates.

For a mean comparison, power depends on an effect in business units relative to variability, sample sizes, allocation and dependence. Decide what effect justifies action, then budget the data needed. Do not invent a “meaningful” effect merely to make the available sample appear adequate.

Pause and explain

If power is 70% at a particular alternative, is every nonsignificant result proof the effect is absent?

Compare your reasoning

No. Even when that alternative is true, the design fails to reject about 30% of the time under its assumptions.

The retail case generates 40 fictional products with an offline and online quote for each product at the same time and under the same assumed quantity and tax definition. Product base prices vary widely. Pairing uses the product, not arbitrary row order.

What is the independent unit for the paired test in this example?

The product-level difference. The two prices within a product are deliberately related and must remain paired.

Pause and explain

Does a mean difference of zero imply every product has equal prices?

Compare your reasoning

No. Positive and negative product differences can cancel. The mean is one summary of the difference distribution, not an equality statement for every pair.

Stop 19 / 24

Measure the mean difference in standard errors

A paired t test is a one-sample t test on dᵢ = onlineᵢ − offlineᵢ. Under a zero-mean null, divide the sample mean difference by its SE. With independent normally distributed differences, the statistic follows a t distribution with n − 1 degrees of freedom under the null.

t = (d̄ − 0)/(s_d/√n); paired 95% CI = d̄ ± t₀.₉₇₅,ₙ₋₁ × s_d/√n
Paired test calculated from the generated raw pairs

The p-value compares the magnitude |t| with both tails of the null t distribution. Pairing can improve precision because stable product-level differences in price level cancel. That benefit depends on preserving correct matches and a defensible independence structure across products.

Pause and explain

What error results from pairing one product’s online quote with another product’s offline quote?

Compare your reasoning

The differences no longer represent the intended matched comparison. Both the estimand and the uncertainty calculation become misleading.

Stop 20 / 24

A significant average difference is not a universal price claim

The paired 95% interval, 0.354 to 1.223 CU, excludes zero. Under the authored paired model, that supports a nonzero average channel difference. It does not say every online quote is higher, that the gap is important, or that switching channels causes this difference in a real population.

An interval makes the magnitude visible. Compare its range with a decision-relevant tolerance established before inspecting results. Also separate uncertainty about the population average from variability across individual products. A narrow mean interval can coexist with large positive and negative individual differences.

For a real operational recommendation, consider transaction fees, travel or delivery costs, availability, timing and the relevant product mix. These can dominate a small average quote difference. The synthetic exercise deliberately excludes those complications so the statistical distinction stays visible.

Pause and explain

Can a statistically detectable difference still be too small to matter operationally?

Compare your reasoning

Yes. A test against exactly zero can reject even when the plausible mean differences all lie within a prespecified practically negligible range.

Stop 21 / 24

Use an independent-groups method when pairing is absent

A separate queue example has two independent groups, with different sample sizes and variances. No natural one-to-one match exists. Welch’s t method estimates uncertainty without forcing equal population variances. A paired test would invent relationships that the design does not contain.

SE(x̄_A − x̄_B) = √(s_A²/n_A + s_B²/n_B); use Welch–Satterthwaite degrees of freedom
Independent synthetic queue samples
QuantityGroup AGroup B
n2230
Mean11.703213.3564

The estimated A − B difference is -1.6533, SE 0.6152, with 48.263 approximate degrees of freedom. The t statistic is -2.6872, two-sided p-value 0.00985, and 95% CI -2.8901 to -0.4164. The full formula and raw sample generation are in the lab.

Welch’s method allows unequal variances; it does not repair dependence, severe distributional problems or a biased comparison. Noninteger degrees of freedom are expected from the approximation.

Pause and explain

Should two groups be paired just because both have measurements in the same units?

Compare your reasoning

No. Pairing comes from the collection design or a justified matching process, not shared units or a convenient spreadsheet layout.

Stop 22 / 24

Set direction and a practical-equivalence margin in advance

Testing “different from zero” is not the same as testing “small enough to treat as practically equivalent.” Equivalence uses a prespecified margin ±Δ. The two one-sided tests (TOST) reject mean ≤ −Δ and mean ≥ +Δ. At α = 0.05, both must reject; equivalently, a compatible 90% two-sided CI must lie strictly within the margin.

Practical margin: −1.50 < μ_difference < +1.50 CU; 90% CI: [0.427, 1.150]

For the synthetic paired case, the two one-sided p-values are 2.05e-13 and 0.0009974. Both are below 0.05, and the 90% CI is inside ±1.50 CU. This supports equivalence of the average under the declared margin, while the 95% CI still excludes zero. There is no contradiction: “nonzero” and “practically small” can both be true.

The margin is an authored teaching choice, not a discovered business standard. In practice it must come from consequences, measurement resolution or an accepted policy before the data are inspected. Equivalence of the mean is not interchangeability for every product.

Pause and explain

Why is a nonsignificant ordinary difference test not enough to show equivalence?

Compare your reasoning

Its interval may be wide enough to include both large beneficial and large harmful differences. Equivalence requires ruling out effects beyond a meaningful margin, not merely failing to reject zero.

Stop 23 / 24

Control the family, not just one reported p-value

With 20 independent true-null tests at α = 0.05, the probability of at least one false rejection is 1 − 0.95²⁰ = 64.2%. Dependence changes that exact calculation, but repeated searching still changes the inferential procedure. The family includes relevant unreported tests, outcomes and analytic variants, not only the final table.

Authored synthetic p-values and recomputed Holm adjustment
Hypothetical testRaw pHolm-adjusted pReject at family α=.05?
Test 10.0030.015Yes
Test 20.0180.072No
Test 30.0410.123No
Test 40.2200.440No
Test 50.6100.610No

For five tests, Bonferroni compares each raw p-value with 0.010. Holm orders p-values and uses a step-down rule, controlling familywise error under arbitrary dependence. Its adjusted p-values are made monotone before returning them to original order. The lab calculates this explicitly.

False discovery rate procedures address a different target: the expected proportion of false rejections among rejections, under their assumptions. Preregister primary questions, label exploration and validate discovered patterns in new data. A multiplicity correction cannot repair undisclosed selective reporting by itself.

Pause and explain

Does reporting only the smallest p-value erase the other tests from the analysis family?

Compare your reasoning

No. The search that produced the selected result determines the error risk. Suppressing the other tests hides rather than removes multiplicity.

Stop 24 / 24

Separate the estimate, uncertainty and decision

A defensible inference brief names the target, observation unit, design, exclusions, estimator and uncertainty method. It distinguishes the statistical result from the operational recommendation and states the assumptions most likely to change the conclusion.

Choose an inferential method from the claim and design
QuestionMethod and caution
One population meant interval when justified; check IID and distribution
One probabilityBinomial/Wilson methods; define event and dependence
Matched comparisonAnalyze differences; preserve pair identity
Independent meansWelch method; do not invent pairing
Practical equivalencePrespecified margin and TOST, not a failed zero test
Many questionsDefine the family and control the relevant error target

Example handoff: “For 40 independently generated matched products, online minus offline averages 0.788 CU (95% CI 0.354 to 1.223). The mean is detectably nonzero and also falls within a prespecified ±1.50 CU equivalence margin under TOST. This concerns an average in an authored synthetic model, not all products or real retailers.”

Before acting, ask four questions: Is the target clear? Does the design support it? Is the uncertainty method matched to the estimator and dependence? Would the plausible effect change the decision? Continue to regression with those questions intact.

Pause and explain

What makes a statistically correct computation an incomplete recommendation?

Compare your reasoning

A missing target population, unsupported design assumption, unexamined practical consequence or hidden analysis search can make the computation irrelevant to the decision even when its arithmetic is correct.
